records.quote:
Gunpowder! Of
course--he had heard Corio mention pirates and their treasure, and
this had been their cache of explosive.
records.paraphrase: Cliff identifies the kegs as pirate gunpowder and conceives a plan to use it.

records.quote:
Before sunrise they must be in
their tombs under the castle, to sleep until another night.
records.paraphrase: The narration explains the vampires' need to return to their tombs before sunrise.

records.quote:
The marrow melted from Cliff Darrell's bones. What--what could he do
against a power that did _that_ to Les Starke?
records.paraphrase: Cliff reacts with fear and helplessness at the power controlling his friend.

records.quote:
At that moment they saw the barrier
of rock like a skull split and sink into the sea. Beyond, cleansing
tongues of flame licked the sky.
records.paraphrase: The island's skull-shaped rock splits and sinks amid fire as it is destroyed.

records.quote:
Down there somewhere were
their graves--graves rent and broken by the explosion--graves
threatened by the flames--and panic had seized the vampires, fear of
the death which would result with exile from their tombs!
records.paraphrase: Cliff deduces the vampires depend on their tombs and flee when the graves are destroyed.

records.quote:
It's--it's--it _can't_ be, damn it!--but it's a
galley, a ship from the days of Alexander the Great! What's it
doing--here--_now_?
records.paraphrase: An ancient galley from the era of Alexander the Great appears in the present day, described as out of its own time.

records.quote:
Out of the winding-sheet of fog into the moonlight crept a strange,
strange craft, her crumbling timbers blackened and rotted with
incredible age. The corpse of a ship, she seemed, resurrected from the
grave of the sea.
records.paraphrase: An impossibly ancient, decayed ship emerges intact and moving from the fog.

records.quote:
all, _all_ were a bloodless white, the skin of
their faces puffed and bloated and horribly wrinkled, like flesh that
had been under water a long time.
records.paraphrase: The galley's crew are drowned-looking, bloodless corpses that nonetheless move.

records.quote:
A drop of my blood in your veins,
and you will belong to the Master, as I do.
records.paraphrase: Corio explains that introducing his blood transforms a person into a servant of the Master.

records.quote:
Those Persian sailors were armed! Their swords and knives were real,
for they cut flesh! Somewhere among their bones must lie sharp-edged
blades!
records.paraphrase: Cliff reasons from observed facts to deduce a means of escape.

records.quote:
we entered into a pact with
the--Master, a pact sealed with blood. In exchange for our lives we
three were to bring other humans to this island for the feasting of
the dead-alive.
records.paraphrase: Corio explains the arrangement by which captives are brought as food for the undead.

records.quote:
An earthquake! The
explosions had jarred the none-too-stable understrata of rock into
spasmodic motion that must grind everything to bits! The island was
doomed!
records.paraphrase: The explosions trigger an earthquake that destroys the entire island.

records.quote:
Vilma Bradley shuddered and shrank against Clifford Darrell's brawny
form. "It's--it's ghastly, Cliff!" she said.
records.paraphrase: Vilma reacts with dread and foreboding to the eerie scene.

records.quote:
Every third month each of us must return with our
cargo when the moon is full; and since we come back on alternating
months, they have a constant supply of fresh blood.
records.paraphrase: Corio describes the scheduled system that keeps the undead supplied with blood.

records.quote:
Dead men ... men whose movements were stiffly wooden ... as dead as
their faces. But most horrible was the fact that they were there, that
they moved at all!
records.paraphrase: The narration emphasizes horror at the moving dead crew.

criteria.rationale: The story is supernatural horror (vampires, undead, blood pacts). The pseudo-explanations offered (blood transforms victims, undead must return to tombs) are occult lore, not scientific facts, theories, discoveries, natural processes, or speculative sciences. No material scientific content is present.

The gunpowder Cliff uses is ordinary historical explosive, and the silver horn is a magical/occult instrument rather than an engineered invention that speculatively affects the setting. These are conventional or supernatural objects, not a science-fictional device, technique, or invention.

An ancient galley from the era of Alexander the Great and its Persian crew persist into the present day, explicitly framed as out of their own time. This evokes temporal displacement, but it is presented as supernatural undeath/preservation rather than genuine time travel, so materiality and interpretation are uncertain.

The narrative does not develop systematic consequences from an identifiable scientific, technological, social, or historical premise. The blood-feast arrangement is described as a fixed supernatural pact, not an extrapolated chain of consequences from a rational premise.

Cliff reasons from observations (the sailors' blades cut flesh, so real blades lie among the bones; the vampires depend on their tombs) to deduce means of escape. This is everyday practical inference under duress rather than sustained scientific method with hypothesis and testing, so materiality is limited.

The isolated Isle of the Undead with its dead forest, skull-shaped rock, and castle of undead is a substantially nonordinary environment populated by supernatural visitors from the past. It reads as a Gothic/horror locale rather than a cosmic or extraterrestrial place, making the science-fictional character uncertain.

The climax features a large-scale disaster: explosions trigger an earthquake that grinds the island to bits, the skull-rock barrier splits and sinks, and the whole island is destroyed by fire and seismic collapse. This catastrophe is actual and causally central to the resolution.

candidates.description: An immortal cult of vampire 'Masters' and their undead servants on a hidden island, sustained by a systematized blood-supply operation in which human agents (Corio and two others) periodically deliver captive humans on alternating months so the dead-alive have a constant supply of fresh blood, in exchange for gold, gems, and extended life.

novelty.rationale: The story posits a totalizing difference from the empirical norm: an island populated by centuries-old undead and vampire Masters served by an ancient resurrected galley crewed by animated corpses, a world-altering supernatural order sustained across historical eras. This alters the crucial aspect of the story universe.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The undead, vampire Masters, blasphemous Latin incantations, animated skeletons, and blood-magic are presented as overtly supernatural and demonic rather than as an immanent, nonsupernatural, systematic account. The 'rules' (must return to tombs before sunrise, a drop of blood binds one to the Master, chilling Presence and incantation) function as occult/horror conventions, not imaginary science or coherent social organization grounded in a nonsupernatural logic. Suvin's cognition requirement is failed.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The undead blood-economy governs the entire narrative logic: the abduction, the island, the torture ceremony, the captives' fate, the climax, and the island's destruction all flow from it. It is not incidental.

estrangement.rationale: Readers encounter a decayed galley from the age of Alexander manned by bloodless drowned corpses appearing in the present, and a scheduled blood-tribute economy, contrasted sharply against the modern yacht party and radio dance orchestra. Characters react with dread and horror.

candidates.description: Corio's four-piped silver horn producing distinct tonal notes that can awaken the undead crew, induce paralysis-sleep in living humans, and irresistibly lure victims with promises of earthly dominion.

novelty.rationale: The horn exhibits an unusual, quasi-hypnotic power over both the living and the dead, but it operates as an instrument within the broader supernatural undead order rather than constituting a distinct world-altering difference on its own.

cognitive_validation.rationale: Its effects (commanding the undead, luring souls, promising dominion) are magical/occult and given no immanent nonsupernatural mechanism.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The horn is a recurring plot device serving the antagonist, but it is an instrument subordinate to the undead-cult premise; it does not itself determine the overriding narrative logic.

estrangement.rationale: The horn's ability to summon corpses and enslave the will is an eerie contrast to any ordinary instrument, but it reads as a magical gadget within an occult framework.
